title: What If You Had a Hummingbird's Metabolism? 🤔
description:
Gus wakes up burning energy like a hummingbird. The food is only his second-biggest problem: this is what physics says happens to the heat.

The numbers, for a 70 kg (154 lb) man with a hummingbird's energy use per gram:
• About 120,000 calories a day: a 250-calorie hamburger every three minutes, day and night (other hummingbird species give up to 155,000)
• Fifty times a normal man's 2,400 calories
• Heart rate of a hummingbird in flight: about 1,200 beats a minute, twenty a second
• Almost 6,000 watts of heat, as much as four 1,500-watt space heaters
• Pound for pound a hummingbird has about twenty times more skin to lose heat through (18 to 25 times, depending on how you measure)
• Even sweating as hard as a human can, he would warm up by more than 1 °C (about 2 °F) every minute
• Cool sea water can carry that heat away. Air cannot.
(Assumption: energy use scales with body mass, gram for gram. Real animals of human size run far slower, for exactly this reason.)

Sources:
• Powers & Nagy, "Field metabolic rate and food consumption by free-living Anna's hummingbirds", Physiological Zoology 61, 500 (1988)
• Powers & Conley, "Field metabolic rate and food consumption of two sympatric hummingbird species", The Condor 96, 141 (1994)
• Lasiewski, Physiological Zoology 37, 212 (1964); Smithsonian National Museum of Natural History (heart rate)
• Xu et al., "The specific heat of the human body", Temperature 10, 235 (2022); Institute of Medicine, Nutritional Needs in Hot Environments (1993) (sweat rates)
• Nadel et al., "Energy exchanges of swimming man", Journal of Applied Physiology 36, 465 (1974)
• Hainsworth & Wolf, Science 168, 368 (1970) (torpor)

Every number is computed in code and checked. Animation, narration and music are made with software and AI tools.
